title: The Nursing Home Plants
text:
In the mid 1970s the psychologists Ellen Langer and Judith Rodin ran a field experiment in a Connecticut nursing home. The residents of two floors were similar in health and background. The administrator gave a short talk to each floor.

To one floor he stressed the residents' own responsibility. They could decide how their rooms were arranged, how to spend their time, and whether and when to complain about anything they disliked. Each resident was offered a small plant and told it was theirs to choose and to take care of. They could also choose which night to see a film. To the other floor, the talk stressed that the staff were there to take care of them. They were handed plants, told that the nurses would water them, and assigned a film night.

Three weeks later, residents on the responsibility floor were rated by nurses who did not know about the study as more alert and active, and they reported feeling happier. They attended more activities and took part more. In a follow-up eighteen months later, Rodin and Langer reported that fewer of the residents from the responsibility floor had died than from the comparison floor.
lesson: Doing everything for people can drain their vitality. Give the people you lead real choices and something of their own to be responsible for.
location: Arden House nursing home, Connecticut, USA
source: Langer, E. J., and Rodin, J. (1976). The effects of choice and enhanced personal responsibility for the aged: A field experiment in an institutional setting. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 34(2), 191-198.
caveat: The sample was small, and the mortality follow-up in particular involved few deaths, so that finding should be held loosely.
